kunyah: Umm Sulaym — mother of Anas ibn Malik
tribe: Ansar — Banu Adi ibn an-Najjar of the Khazraj
era: The Woman Whose Dowry Was Islam
teaser: She set his Islam as the price of marrying her. And the night her son died, she said nothing until morning.

layers.title: Who She Was
layers.subtitle: A Madinan family that gave up almost everyone
layers.content:
Ibn Sa'd sets out the family twice, because two of its men have their own entries among the people of Badr. Her father Milhan's given name was Malik ibn Khalid ibn Zayd ibn Haram, of Banu Adi ibn an-Najjar, a clan of the Khazraj in Madinah. Her mother was Mulaykah bint Malik.

Her brothers were Haram ibn Milhan and Sulaym ibn Milhan. Both were at Badr. Both were at Uhud. Both were killed on the same day at Bi'r Ma'unah, and Ibn Sa'd closes each entry with the same flat sentence: he has no descendants. He adds that the line of Khalid ibn Zayd ibn Haram has died out, and there is no one left.

Her sister was Umm Haram, the wife of Ubadah ibn as-Samit. Her son was Anas ibn Malik, who would serve the Prophet ﷺ for a decade and become one of the most prolific narrators in Islam.

Reports differ on her own given name — ar-Rumaysa is the one most often transmitted, and others are offered. She is remembered by her kunya, which is what people actually called her.

So: an Ansari woman from a family that produced two of the Badr companions and lost both, whose sister married a chief of the Ansar, and whose son grew up in the Prophet's ﷺ own service.
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab at-Tabaqat al-Kabir, Vol. III, trans. Aisha Bewley — the entries on Haram ibn Milhan and Sulaym ibn Milhan

layers.title: The Conversion
layers.subtitle: She named her price and it was not money
layers.content:
The Ansar came to Islam early in Madinah, and she was among them. What the sources preserve about her belief is not the moment she accepted it but the moment she made someone else pay for access to her.

Abu Talhah Zayd ibn Sahl came to propose. He was one of the notable men of the Khazraj and he was not yet a Muslim. Sunan an-Nasa'i carries the exchange, narrated through her son Anas.

She told him that the thing he worshipped was wood, grown from the earth, carved by a craftsman of such-and-such a family, and that it could neither harm nor help him. If he became Muslim, she said, that would be her dowry, and she would ask him for nothing else.

He became Muslim, and that was her mahr. The transmitter Thabit adds the line that made the report famous among the scholars: he had never heard of a woman whose dowry was nobler than Umm Sulaym's — Islam.

Reports also state that her first husband, Malik, the father of Anas, died outside Islam. Hold the two facts side by side and the second marriage stops looking like a romance and starts looking like a decision made by someone who had already watched the alternative.

She was not converting a suitor for the sake of a wedding. She was refusing to be married into a house that worshipped a piece of wood.
layers.hadith_ref: Sunan an-Nasa'i, Book of Marriage — narrated by Anas ibn Malik: 'If you become Muslim, that will be my dowry' (not carried in Ibn Sa'd Vol. III)
layers.source: Sunan an-Nasa'i, narrated by Anas ibn Malik — not in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III, which covers the men of Badr

layers.title: With the Prophet ﷺ
layers.subtitle: The brotherhood of Madinah was sworn in her house
layers.content:
There is a line in Vol. III that most readers pass over. When the Prophet ﷺ arrived in Madinah, the Muhajirun had been cut off from their relatives and were in a city with no tribal ties of their own. So he paired them, one Muhajir to one Ansari, and they inherited from one another. Ibn Sa'd records where it happened: this took place in the house of Umm Sulaym bint Milhan. He told them, let each of you take a brother in Allah.

The act that turned two frightened groups into one community was performed in her front room.

Her household stayed close after that. Her husband Abu Talhah shielded the Prophet ﷺ with his own chest at Uhud; Anas reports that he broke two or three bows that day, and that when a man went past with a full quiver the Prophet ﷺ would say, give the arrows to Abu Talhah. Her son Anas served him for ten years. She is quoted on something only someone in the room could know — that his sweat smelled better than the finest perfume.

And she was not only a hostess. Sahih Muslim records that at Hunayn she was carrying a dagger. Asked what it was for, she said that if a mushrik came near her she would open his belly with it.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih Muslim, Book of Jihad — narrated by Anas ibn Malik: Umm Sulaym carried a dagger on the day of Hunayn
layers.source: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III — the section on the Brotherhood; al-Mubarakpuri, The Sealed Nectar — Abu Talhah at Uhud, and Umm Sulaym on the Prophet's ﷺ scent; Sahih Muslim for Hunayn

layers.title: The Trial
layers.subtitle: She let her husband eat before she told him
layers.content:
This is one of the most extraordinary narrations in the whole corpus, and it is in both Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, transmitted by her son Anas.

A son of hers by Abu Talhah fell ill and died while Abu Talhah was away. She washed the boy, shrouded him, laid him down, and told the household not to say a word to his father until she said it herself.

Abu Talhah came home and asked how the boy was. She said he was more at rest than he had been. She put his supper in front of him, and he ate and drank. She made herself beautiful for him, more than she ever had, and they passed the night as husband and wife.

In the morning she asked him a question. If some people lent a thing to a household, and then asked for their loan back, would that household have the right to refuse it? He said no, of course not. Then she said: your son has died.

He was angry. You left me, he said, until I was in that state, and then you told me. He went out to the Prophet ﷺ and reported it, and the Prophet ﷺ said: may Allah bless the night the two of you spent together.

Read what she actually did. She carried the death alone for a whole night so that her husband could eat one more meal without it.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim — narrated by Anas ibn Malik: 'May Allah bless the night you spent together' (not carried in Ibn Sa'd Vol. III)
layers.source: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by Anas ibn Malik — not in Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III

layers.title: The Legacy
layers.subtitle: Nine grandsons, and footsteps heard in the Garden
layers.content:
The same narration finishes the account. She conceived from that night, and bore a son, and the Prophet ﷺ named him Abdullah. The transmitters add what became of him: one of the Ansar said he saw nine sons of that Abdullah, and every one of them had memorised the Qur'an.

Count the arithmetic of the night she stayed silent. One child buried, one child given, nine grandsons carrying the Book.

Her brothers had gone the other way. Anas describes Bi'r Ma'unah plainly: the Prophet ﷺ sent seventy of the Ansar, the ones called the reciters, who studied by night and drew water and sold firewood by day to feed the poor of the mosque. His uncle Haram went ahead to give them the message and was speared through, and said: Allah is greater, I have won, by the Lord of the Ka'bah. They killed all of them but one lame man. Her other brother Sulaym died in the same place on the same day.

Sahih Muslim carries a saying of the Prophet ﷺ that he entered the Garden and heard footsteps, and asked whose they were, and was told: the mother of Anas ibn Malik.

What the ummah kept from Umm Sulaym, may Allah be pleased with her, is a hard and unfashionable idea: that composure is a form of mercy. She was not cold on the night her son died. She was carrying it so that someone else would not have to yet.
layers.hadith_ref: Sahih Muslim, Book of the Virtues of the Companions — the Prophet ﷺ heard footsteps in the Garden and was told they belonged to the mother of Anas ibn Malik; reports differ on her given name
layers.source: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by Anas ibn Malik; Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III — the entries on Haram and Sulaym ibn Milhan and Bi'r Ma'unah

quiz.prompt: What did Umm Sulaym ask for as her dowry when Abu Talhah proposed to her?

options.text: A house of her own in Madinah
Nothing at all, out of modesty
That he become Muslim
Forty dirhams and a she-camel

quiz.citation: Sunan an-Nasa'i, Book of Marriage — narrated by Anas ibn Malik
quiz.scholar_reflection: She told him the thing he worshipped was carved wood that could neither harm nor help him. The transmitter Thabit said he had never heard of a nobler dowry than hers.

quiz.prompt: According to Ibn Sa'd's Vol. III, what happened in the house of Umm Sulaym bint Milhan?

options.text: The first Friday prayer in Madinah was held
The Prophet ﷺ paired the Muhajirun and Ansar as brothers
The treaty with the tribes of Madinah was written
The qibla was changed towards the Ka'bah

quiz.citation: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III — the section on the Brotherhood
quiz.scholar_reflection: He told them, let each of you take a brother in Allah, and they inherited from one another until the ayat of inheritance came down after Badr. The act that fused the community happened under her roof.

quiz.prompt: What did she do on the night her son died, while Abu Talhah was away?

options.text: Sent word to him immediately by messenger
Went to the Prophet ﷺ before telling anyone else
Washed and shrouded the boy and told the household to say nothing until she spoke
Buried him at once with her brothers

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim — narrated by Anas ibn Malik
quiz.scholar_reflection: She fed her husband, spent the night as his wife, and told him in the morning by way of a question about a loan being reclaimed. He was angry. The Prophet ﷺ blessed the night.

quiz.prompt: What happened to her two brothers, Haram and Sulaym ibn Milhan?

options.text: They were killed on the same day at Bi'r Ma'unah
They were killed at Uhud beside the Prophet ﷺ
They died of plague in Syria
They survived and settled in Basra

quiz.citation: Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III — the entries on Haram ibn Milhan and Sulaym ibn Milhan; narrated from Anas ibn Malik
quiz.scholar_reflection: Both were at Badr and Uhud first. Haram was speared while delivering the Prophet's ﷺ message and said, Allah is greater, I have won, by the Lord of the Ka'bah. Ibn Sa'd notes the family line died out entirely.

quiz.prompt: What was Umm Sulaym carrying on the day of Hunayn?

options.text: The banner of the Khazraj
A dagger
Her infant son
Water for the wounded only

quiz.citation: Sahih Muslim, Book of Jihad — narrated by Anas ibn Malik
quiz.scholar_reflection: Asked what it was for, she said that if a mushrik came near her she would open his belly with it. The same woman who fed her husband his supper in silence was armed on a battlefield.

quiz.prompt: She made someone's belief the condition of access to her life. Where do you hold a line about who you let close?

options.text: On faith and character, and I do not bend
I have lines, but I have moved them before
I am more forgiving than is good for me
I have never had to say no to anything this large

quiz.citation: Sunan an-Nasa'i, narrated by Anas ibn Malik
quiz.scholar_reflection: She was a widow with a young son in a city where a proposal from a notable man was security. She still named a condition she could not be talked out of.

quiz.prompt: She carried a death alone for one night so her husband could eat in peace. When you get bad news, what is your instinct with it?

options.text: Tell people straight away — carrying it alone is worse
Wait for the right moment, even if it costs me
I go quiet and end up telling nobody for too long
It depends on whether they can act on it

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by Anas ibn Malik
quiz.scholar_reflection: Her husband's first reaction was anger at being kept in the dark. The Prophet's ﷺ reaction was a blessing on the night. Both responses are recorded, and the report keeps them both.

quiz.prompt: The community was welded together in her front room, and her name is barely attached to it. How comfortable are you being the venue rather than the event?

options.text: Completely — I like making the space for things
I want to be in the room, not just own it
I would do it, but I would want it remembered
I have never thought of hosting as a contribution

quiz.citation: Reflection on Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III — the Brotherhood in the house of Umm Sulaym
quiz.scholar_reflection: The pairing of the Muhajirun and Ansar is one of the hinges of Islamic history. It needed a floor, a roof, and someone willing to have that many people in her home.

quiz.prompt: Her family lost two brothers at Bi'r Ma'unah and its line ended entirely. What do you do with a loss that has no compensation attached?

options.text: Look for the meaning and usually find one
Accept that some losses are simply losses
I struggle badly when there is nothing to learn
Keep the names alive and leave the rest to Allah

quiz.citation: Reflection on Bi'r Ma'unah — Ibn Sa'd, Tabaqat, Vol. III, narrated from Anas ibn Malik
quiz.scholar_reflection: Her brother's last words were that he had won. Ibn Sa'd's last words on the family are that there is no one left. The sources hold both without resolving them.

quiz.prompt: One buried child, one child given, nine grandsons who memorised the Qur'an. What are you willing to invest in without seeing the return?

options.text: Family — that is where I put everything
Work whose results outlive me
I want to see results, and I know that limits me
Whatever I am asked for, without calculating

quiz.citation: Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, narrated by Anas ibn Malik — the account of Abdullah and his nine sons
quiz.scholar_reflection: She could not have known any of that on the night she stayed silent. She was simply making one more evening bearable for one man.
